title: Multi-scale Low-dose Cryogenic TEM for Probing Beam-sensitive Thin-film Ionomer Variability Across Electrodes in Hydrogen Devices
content: Low-dose cryogenic (scanning) transmission electron microscopy (cryo-(S)TEM) has emerged as a vital tool for investigating beam-sensitive materials in both the biological and physical science communities by preserving them in a near-native state while minimizing damage from electron beam exposure [1-3]. This technique is crucial for studying highly sensitive proton-conducting ionomer materials in electrodes of hydrogen devices, where challenges such as rapid beam-induced motion [4-6] and damage [7, 8] impede acquisition of high-resolution, reproducible data with high integrity. While conventional low-dose cryo-TEM methods show promise for addressing some of these challenges [9-12], additional methods are needed to provide a comprehensive understanding of the spatial variations of ionomer properties across full electrode structures, which is vital for optimizing electrode design and enhancing cell performance and durability [13-15]. Finally, conventional sample preparation methods, such as ultramicrotome methods involving epoxy, impede the ability to image ionomer thin-films within electrodes. Addressing these issues is key to achieving reliable, statistical insights into ionomer properties within hydrogen device electrode structures and accelerating development of durable, high-performance cells.
